alabama.appeal_deadline: File a written objection with your County Board of Equalization within 30 calendar days of the date printed on your valuation notice, or by the first Monday in July, whichever is later; the exact window varies by county because each county mails notices on its own schedule.
alabama.appeal_where: County Board of Equalization, reached through your county Revenue Commissioner or appraisal office; start with an informal review with the assessor if your county offers one.
alabama.appeal_how: Contact the assessor informally first, then file a written objection with the Board of Equalization stating the property description and your reasons; the board holds a hearing and rules on the value.
alabama.appeal_evidence: Recent comparable sales of similar nearby homes, a recent independent appraisal, photos showing condition problems, and errors in the assessor's record such as wrong square footage or lot size.
alabama.appeal_fee: No fee to file with the Board of Equalization; a Circuit Court appeal may involve court costs.
alabama.after_appeal: Appeal to Circuit Court within 30 days of the board's final decision; you must file notice with both the board secretary and the circuit clerk, post a cost bond, and pay the taxes before they become delinquent or post a supersedeas bond.

alaska.appeal_deadline: File a written appeal with your local Board of Equalization within 30 days of the date your assessment notice was mailed; notices go out at different times by borough, from February in Anchorage to April in smaller boroughs.
alaska.appeal_where: Your city or borough assessor for an informal review, then the local Board of Equalization.
alaska.appeal_how: Ask the assessor to correct any error first, then submit a written appeal on the prescribed form to the Board of Equalization; you carry the burden of proving the value is excessive, unequal, or improper.
alaska.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an independent appraisal, photos of the property's condition, and proof of errors in the assessor's records; the board cannot raise your assessment unless you ask for a review.
alaska.after_appeal: Appeal the board's decision to Alaska Superior Court within 30 days of the date the decision was mailed or sent.

arizona.appeal_deadline: File a petition for review with your county assessor within 60 days of the date the Notice of Value was mailed, usually in late February to April; the exact date is printed on your notice.
arizona.appeal_where: County assessor first (a required first step), then the County Board of Equalization, or the State Board of Equalization in Maricopa and Pima counties.
arizona.appeal_how: File a petition for review (Form 82130R for residential property) with the county assessor; if denied, appeal to the county or State Board of Equalization, then to Tax Court.
arizona.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales from your county's public sales records, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's property record; note Arizona taxes you on limited property value, not full cash value.
arizona.after_appeal: Appeal a Board of Equalization decision to the State Board of Equalization within 25 days of the date the decision was mailed (Maricopa and Pima counties), then to Arizona Tax Court within 60 days of the State Board's final decision; a direct Tax Court filing is also allowed by December 15.

arkansas.appeal_deadline: Apply to your County Equalization Board on or before the third Monday in August every year; the deadline applies whether or not you received a notice, since notices only go out when your value changes.
arkansas.appeal_where: County Equalization Board, through its secretary; start with an informal review with the county assessor before the August deadline.
arkansas.appeal_how: Apply in person, by petition, or by letter to the secretary of the County Equalization Board; the board begins hearings no later than the second Monday in August and notifies you in writing of its decision.
arkansas.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales showing your home's market value is lower, photos of condition or needed repairs, and errors in the assessor's records; give the assessor any new evidence at least five business days before the hearing.
arkansas.after_appeal: Appeal to County Court by filing a petition with the county clerk on or before the second Monday in October; the court must hear and decide the case by November 15.

california.appeal_deadline: File Form BOE-305-AH with the clerk of the board between July 2 and September 15 in counties that mail value notices to all owners by August 1, or July 2 to November 30 in most other counties; supplemental and escape assessments have a 60-day deadline from the notice.
california.appeal_where: Your county Assessment Appeals Board, through the clerk of the board of supervisors; start with an informal review with the county assessor.
california.appeal_how: File an Assessment Appeal Application (Form BOE-305-AH) with the clerk of the board; the board holds a hearing and must decide within two years of a timely filing unless you agree to an extension.
california.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales near the January 1 lien date (the board may not consider sales more than 90 days after that date), an appraisal, and proof of errors in the assessor's records; most residential appeals argue a decline in value under Proposition 8.
california.appeal_fee: Varies by county, typically $40 to $50 (for example, $50 in Alameda County, $40 in Contra Costa County, and $46 in Los Angeles County).
california.after_appeal: The Assessment Appeals Board is the final administrative step; further relief is through the courts, so read the board's decision letter for the deadline and procedure.

colorado.appeal_deadline: Protest to your county assessor from May 1, when notices of valuation are mailed; the deadline is June 1 starting with the 2027 cycle (it was June 8 in earlier years), so confirm the date on your notice.
colorado.appeal_where: County assessor first, then the County Board of Equalization, then the state Board of Assessment Appeals, district court, or binding arbitration.
colorado.appeal_how: File a written protest with the county assessor; if denied, petition the County Board of Equalization by July 15 in most counties or September 15 in the nine large counties on the alternate procedure.
colorado.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales from the assessor's own sales study period, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the property record such as wrong square footage or features.
colorado.appeal_fee: No fee to protest to the county assessor.
colorado.after_appeal: Within 30 days of the County Board's decision being mailed, appeal to the state Board of Assessment Appeals, file in district court for a new trial, or choose binding arbitration.

connecticut.appeal_deadline: File a written appeal with your town's Board of Assessment Appeals on or before February 20 (March 20 in towns where the assessor got an extension); the appeal must be in the board's hands by that date, not just postmarked.
connecticut.appeal_where: Town assessor for an informal review, then the town Board of Assessment Appeals.
connecticut.appeal_how: Ask the assessor to correct the value first, then file a written appeal with the Board of Assessment Appeals; the board holds hearings in March (or April in extended-deadline towns) and notifies you in writing.
connecticut.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales of similar homes, an appraisal, photos of condition problems, and errors in the assessor's record; Connecticut assesses at 70% of fair market value, so argue the full market value.
connecticut.after_appeal: Appeal to Connecticut Superior Court within two months of the date the board mails its decision; the court hears the case fresh and decides the property's true value itself.

delaware.appeal_deadline: File a written appeal with your county Board of Assessment Review before March 15 each year (New Castle County accepts forms January 1 through March 14); Kent County's annual deadline is January 31, so confirm the exact date and hour with your county.
delaware.appeal_where: Your county Board of Assessment Review, filed through the county assessment office; start with an informal review with the assessor.
delaware.appeal_how: Complete your county's official appeal form and submit it to the county assessment office before the deadline; the board hears appeals in the spring and rules on the value.
delaware.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records.
delaware.after_appeal: Appeal the board's decision to Delaware Superior Court within 30 days of being notified of the decision.

florida.appeal_deadline: File a petition with your county Value Adjustment Board within 25 days of the date the TRIM notice was mailed (usually mid-September); the exact date is printed on the notice, and an informal talk with the appraiser does not extend it.
florida.appeal_where: County Property Appraiser for an informal conference (optional), then the county Value Adjustment Board.
florida.appeal_how: Request an informal conference with the property appraiser if you wish, then file a petition on Department of Revenue Form DR-486 with the Value Adjustment Board; a special magistrate hears the case and recommends a decision.
florida.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales from the prior year, an appraisal, photos of condition or damage, and errors in the appraiser's records; you are contesting just value as of January 1, not the tax rate.
florida.appeal_fee: $15 per parcel, paid to the clerk of court when you file Form DR-486.
florida.after_appeal: Appeal a Value Adjustment Board decision to Circuit Court, or skip the board and file directly in Circuit Court within 60 days of the date the assessment is certified for collection; you must first pay the taxes you admit are owed.

georgia.appeal_deadline: File a written appeal with your County Board of Tax Assessors within 45 days of the date your Annual Notice of Assessment was mailed; the clock runs from the mailing date, not the day you received it.
georgia.appeal_where: County Board of Tax Assessors first, then the County Board of Equalization, a hearing officer, or an arbitrator - you choose one of the three when you file.
georgia.appeal_how: File Form PT-311A or a written notice of appeal with the Board of Tax Assessors; the board may change the value and send a new notice, which you can appeal within 30 days, or the appeal goes to the Board of Equalization for a hearing.
georgia.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales from the prior calendar year only, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; Georgia assesses at 40% of fair market value.
georgia.after_appeal: Appeal the Board of Equalization, hearing officer, or arbitrator decision to Superior Court within 30 days of the date the decision was mailed or hand-delivered.

hawaii.appeal_deadline: Deadlines are set by each county: Honolulu's appeal window is December 15 to January 15; Kauai County accepts appeals December 1 through December 31; Hawaii County and Maui County use April 9.
hawaii.appeal_where: Your county Board of Review, filed through the county Real Property Assessment or Tax office; start with an informal review with the county assessor.
hawaii.appeal_how: File your county's appeal form with the county assessment office during the window; the five-member Board of Review hears the appeal and decides the value.
hawaii.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or damage, and errors in the assessor's records; Honolulu requires showing the value is more than 10% too high, Hawaii County 20%.
hawaii.appeal_fee: Honolulu requires a $50 deposit when filing an appeal; Kauai County charges a $75 fee.
hawaii.after_appeal: Appeal the Board of Review's decision to the Hawaii Tax Appeal Court within 30 days of the date the board's decision was filed.

idaho.appeal_deadline: File a written appeal with your county Board of Equalization by the close of business on the fourth Monday of June (June 22, 2026); assessment notices are mailed no later than the first Monday in June.
idaho.appeal_where: County Board of Equalization (the county commissioners sitting as that board), reached through the county clerk or auditor; start with an informal review with the county assessor.
idaho.appeal_how: File a written appeal on the county's form with the county board of equalization; the board hears appeals and must finish by the second Monday in July.
idaho.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; value is market value as of January 1.
idaho.after_appeal: Within 30 days after the board mails its decision or announces it at the hearing, appeal to the Idaho Board of Tax Appeals or to the district court in the county where the property sits.

illinois.appeal_deadline: Illinois has no single statewide deadline: file with your county Board of Review within 30 days of the date your township's assessments are published; in Cook County, appeal to the assessor within 30 days of the reassessment notice mailing, then to the Board of Review in its township window.
illinois.appeal_where: Township or county assessor for an informal review, then your county Board of Review.
illinois.appeal_how: Contact the township assessor first to fix factual errors, then file a formal appeal with the Board of Review on its prescribed forms with your evidence attached; the board schedules a hearing and issues a written decision.
illinois.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and proof of errors in the assessment records; the board's rules list the evidence required for each ground of appeal.
illinois.after_appeal: Appeal to the state Property Tax Appeal Board (PTAB) within 30 days of the Board of Review's written decision; in Cook County, within 30 days of the decision or of the board's final action on the township, whichever is later.

indiana.appeal_deadline: File Form 130 with your assessing official by June 15 of the assessment year if the notice of assessment was mailed before May 1, or by June 15 of the year the tax bill was mailed if the notice went out on or after May 1.
indiana.appeal_where: Your township or county assessing official first, then the County Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals (PTABOA).
indiana.appeal_how: File Form 130 (Taxpayer's Notice to Initiate an Appeal) with the assessing official for each parcel; filing also requests an informal meeting, and the PTABOA must hold a hearing within 180 days of filing.
indiana.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an independent appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; the value is market value as of January 1.
indiana.after_appeal: File Form 131 with the Indiana Board of Tax Review within 45 days of the PTABOA's order; if the PTABOA issues no decision within 180 days, you may go to the Board of Tax Review directly.

iowa.appeal_deadline: File a written protest with your local Board of Review between April 2 and April 30 each year; if April 30 falls on a weekend, the deadline moves to the next business day.
iowa.appeal_where: County or city assessor for an informal review (April 2 to April 25), then the local Board of Review.
iowa.appeal_how: Request an informal review with the assessor, then file the Petition to the Local Board of Review form in person, by email, or by mail postmarked by April 30; the board meets in May and must finish by May 31.
iowa.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; your evidence must support the value as of the January 1 assessment date and state one of the five grounds in Iowa Code section 441.37.
iowa.after_appeal: Appeal to the state Property Assessment Appeal Board or to district court within 20 days after the later of the board's adjournment or May 31 (about June 20 in a typical year).

kansas.appeal_deadline: Appeal to your county appraiser within 30 days of the date the valuation notice was mailed (notices go out by March 1 for real property); for personal property, appeal by May 15.
kansas.appeal_where: County appraiser for an informal meeting first, then the Kansas Board of Tax Appeals (Small Claims Division for homes) or a county hearing officer panel where one exists.
kansas.appeal_how: Contact the county appraiser within 30 days to schedule an informal meeting; the appraiser must mail the results by May 20, and you then have 30 days (or 18 days to a hearing officer panel) to appeal further.
kansas.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the appraiser's records; the county appraiser must prove the value is correct - no presumption of correctness applies.
kansas.after_appeal: Appeal the Small Claims or hearing officer decision to the full Board of Tax Appeals within 30 days; a Board of Tax Appeals decision can then go to district court for judicial review.

kentucky.appeal_deadline: First have a conference with your Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) during the tax roll inspection period, which normally runs the first Monday in May through the third Monday in May; then file your appeal with the county clerk no later than one workday after the inspection period closes.
kentucky.appeal_where: County Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) for a required conference, then the local Board of Assessment Appeals, filed with the county clerk.
kentucky.appeal_how: Request a conference with the PVA before or during the inspection period; if no agreement is reached, file the appeal form from the county clerk's office, and the three-member local board hears the case.
kentucky.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the PVA's records; Kentucky assesses at 100% of fair cash value as of January 1.
kentucky.after_appeal: Appeal the local board's decision to the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals within 30 days of the date the board's ruling notice was mailed.

louisiana.appeal_deadline: Review the assessment roll during the 15-day public exposure period, typically mid-July to mid-August (Orleans Parish runs July 15 to August 15); file your complaint with the parish Board of Review at least seven days before the board's public hearing.
louisiana.appeal_where: Parish assessor for an informal review, then the parish Board of Review (the parish governing authority sitting as the board).
louisiana.appeal_how: Inspect the roll during the exposure period and talk to the assessor, then file a formal complaint with the Board of Review before its hearing; the board hears the case in September or early October.
louisiana.appeal_evidence: Recent appraisals, comparable sales, photos showing property condition, and contractor repair estimates.
louisiana.after_appeal: Appeal the Board of Review's decision to the Louisiana Tax Commission within 30 days of the board's written decision, following the Commission's filing rule (Form 3103.A); the Commission's decision can then be appealed to district court within 30 days.

maine.appeal_deadline: File a written application for abatement with your local assessor or municipal officers within 185 days of the date the tax was committed (the commitment date is on your tax bill); the deadline is jurisdictional and cannot be waived.
maine.appeal_where: Local assessor or municipal officers for the abatement application, then the local Board of Assessment Review (or the county commissioners if your town has no board).
maine.appeal_how: File the abatement application in writing with the assessor; the assessor has 60 days to decide, and if there is no decision in 60 days the application is deemed denied.
maine.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; the value is as of the April 1 assessment date.
maine.after_appeal: Appeal the assessor's decision to the local Board of Assessment Review (or county commissioners) within 60 days; the board's decision can then be appealed to Superior Court within 30 days.

maryland.appeal_deadline: Appeal to your local Supervisor of Assessments within 45 days of the date on your assessment notice; in the two years your property is not reassessed, you may instead file a Petition for Review by the first business day of January.
maryland.appeal_where: Local Supervisor of Assessments (State Department of Assessments and Taxation) first, then the Property Tax Assessment Appeal Board (PTAAB) in your county.
maryland.appeal_how: File online through the SDAT appeal portal or mail the appeal form to your local SDAT office within 45 days; the supervisor holds an informal hearing, then issues a final notice.
maryland.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales near the January 1 assessment date, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessment records.
maryland.after_appeal: Appeal to the Property Tax Assessment Appeal Board within 30 days of the supervisor's final notice, then to the Maryland Tax Court within 30 days of the board's order.

massachusetts.appeal_deadline: File an abatement application with your local board of assessors by the due date of the first installment of the actual tax bill - usually February 1 in quarterly-billing towns (or May 1, or 30 days after the bills are mailed, if the bills went out after December 31).
massachusetts.appeal_where: Your city or town board of assessors; there is no separate local board hearing before the assessors decide.
massachusetts.appeal_how: File the state abatement form (State Tax Form 128) with the assessors; they have three months to act, and if they do not act the application is deemed denied.
massachusetts.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessors' records; the value is fair cash value as of January 1.
massachusetts.after_appeal: Appeal to the state Appellate Tax Board within three months of the date the assessors granted or denied the abatement, or of the deemed denial date.

michigan.appeal_deadline: Protest to your local March Board of Review - the board meets in March, typically the week of the second Monday, and the exact dates are set by your city or township; the March board is the only local chance to appeal value each year.
michigan.appeal_where: Local assessor for an informal review, then your city or township March Board of Review.
michigan.appeal_how: File a petition (Form L-4035) with the March Board of Review; residential owners must protest there first to keep the right to go to the Michigan Tax Tribunal.
michigan.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; Michigan assesses at 50% of true cash value.
michigan.appeal_fee: No fee to protest at your local Board of Review.
michigan.after_appeal: Petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal by July 31 of the tax year for residential property (commercial and industrial property may file directly with the Tribunal by May 31).

minnesota.appeal_deadline: Attend your Local Board of Appeal and Equalization meeting, held between April 1 and May 31 on the date printed on your valuation notice; the final deadline to petition the Minnesota Tax Court is April 30 of the year the tax becomes payable.
minnesota.appeal_where: County assessor for an informal review or Open Book meeting, then the Local Board of Appeal and Equalization, then the County Board of Appeal and Equalization.
minnesota.appeal_how: Meet with the assessor first, then appear at the Local Board meeting on the date on your notice; you must go to the local board before the County Board will hear you.
minnesota.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records such as wrong square footage, bedrooms, or lot size.
minnesota.after_appeal: Appeal to the Minnesota Tax Court by April 30 of the year the tax becomes payable; you may also go straight to Tax Court without going through the boards, and the Small Claims Division hears cases where the estimated market value is under $300,000.

mississippi.appeal_deadline: File a written objection with your county Board of Supervisors by the first Monday in August each year, when the board holds its equalization meeting; assessment rolls are open for inspection during July.
mississippi.appeal_where: County tax assessor for an informal review, then the County Board of Supervisors acting as the Board of Equalization.
mississippi.appeal_how: Inspect the roll in July, then file a written objection with the clerk of the Board of Supervisors before the August meeting; the board hears objections and can raise or lower values.
mississippi.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; values are set as of January 1.
mississippi.after_appeal: Appeal to circuit court within 20 days of the date the board's notice is mailed; the appeal requires a bond with sureties for double the tax in dispute, with a $100 minimum.

missouri.appeal_deadline: Appeal to your county Board of Equalization by the second Monday in July of the assessment year (some counties use the third Monday in June, and Jackson County has extended its deadline in recent years, so confirm the date with your county clerk).
missouri.appeal_where: County assessor for an informal review, then the County Board of Equalization.
missouri.appeal_how: Talk to the assessor first, then file an appeal form with the county Board of Equalization before its deadline; the board holds a hearing and issues a decision.
missouri.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; Missouri reassesses real property every two years in odd-numbered years.
missouri.appeal_fee: No fee to file a complaint with the State Tax Commission.
missouri.after_appeal: File a Complaint for Review of Assessment with the Missouri State Tax Commission by September 30 of the assessment year or within 30 days of the Board of Equalization's decision, whichever is later.

montana.appeal_deadline: File an appeal with your County Tax Appeal Board within 30 days of the date on your classification and appraisal notice (usually mailed in June), or within 30 days of the Department of Revenue's decision if you first asked for an informal review on Form AB-26.
montana.appeal_where: Montana Department of Revenue for an informal review (Form AB-26), then the County Tax Appeal Board, filed with the county clerk and recorder.
montana.appeal_how: File Form AB-26 with the Department of Revenue, or appeal directly to the County Tax Appeal Board on Form MTAB-401; the county board holds a hearing, generally between July 1 and December 31.
montana.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an independent appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the property record; only one appeal is allowed per two-year appraisal cycle.
montana.after_appeal: Appeal the county board's decision to the Montana Tax Appeal Board within 30 days of receiving it (or within 45 days of the county board hearing, whichever is later); judicial review must then be sought within 60 days of the state board's decision.

nebraska.appeal_deadline: File a protest with the county clerk on Form 422 on or before June 30 of the tax year; change-of-value notices are mailed by June 1.
nebraska.appeal_where: County assessor for an informal review, then the County Board of Equalization, filed with the county clerk.
nebraska.appeal_how: File Form 422 in triplicate with the county clerk, stating your reasons and the value you claim, with supporting documents attached; the board hears protests June 1 through July 25.
nebraska.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; the protest must include documentation justifying the value you claim or it will be dismissed.
nebraska.after_appeal: Appeal to the Tax Equalization and Review Commission (TERC) by August 24, or September 10 in counties that extended their hearings; TERC's order can then be appealed to the Court of Appeals within 30 days.

nevada.appeal_deadline: File a petition with your County Board of Equalization no later than January 15; value notices are mailed by December 18.
nevada.appeal_where: County assessor for an informal review, then the County Board of Equalization.
nevada.appeal_how: File a written petition with the county assessor or county board by January 15; the county board hears appeals in January and February and must finish by the end of February.
nevada.appeal_evidence: An appraisal showing the home would sell for less than its taxable value, comparable sales, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; Nevada values land at full cash value plus improvements at depreciated replacement cost, capped at full cash value.
nevada.after_appeal: Appeal the county board's decision to the Nevada State Board of Equalization by March 10 (postmark counts); after the State Board, the remedy is paying the tax and suing for a refund in district court within three months of the final installment.

new-hampshire.appeal_deadline: File a written application for abatement with your town's assessing officials (selectmen or assessors) by March 1 following the final tax bill; if the tax notice came after December 31, you have two months from the notice instead.
new-hampshire.appeal_where: Municipal board of selectmen or assessors for the abatement application.
new-hampshire.appeal_how: File the abatement application in writing with the town after you receive the final tax bill; the town has until July 1 to grant or deny it.
new-hampshire.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessors' records; you must show the value was wrong as of the April 1 assessment date.
new-hampshire.appeal_fee: A $65 nonrefundable fee is required to appeal to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals.
new-hampshire.after_appeal: If the town denies the abatement or does not act, appeal to the state Board of Tax and Land Appeals or to Superior Court by September 1 - you must choose one, not both; BTLA appeals must be mailed or hand-delivered, not emailed.

new-jersey.appeal_deadline: File with your county Board of Taxation by April 1, or 45 days after the town finishes mailing assessment notices, whichever is later; the deadline is May 1 in a town-wide revaluation or reassessment year, and January 15 in Burlington, Gloucester, and Monmouth counties.
new-jersey.appeal_where: Your county Board of Taxation; properties assessed over $1,000,000 may file directly with the New Jersey Tax Court instead.
new-jersey.appeal_how: File a Petition of Appeal (Form A-1) with the county board, with a comparable sales form; the board holds a hearing and issues a judgment.
new-jersey.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, and photos of condition or defects; New Jersey judges value against the Chapter 123 common level range, which allows a 15% tolerance band around the county's equalization ratio.
new-jersey.appeal_fee: A filing fee applies and varies by county; the amount was not confirmed from an official source.
new-jersey.after_appeal: Appeal a county board judgment to the New Jersey Tax Court within 45 days of the date the judgment was mailed.

new-mexico.appeal_deadline: File a protest petition with your county assessor no later than 30 days after the Notice of Value was mailed (notices usually go out around April 1); the deadline is the later of April 1 or 30 days after mailing.
new-mexico.appeal_where: County assessor for the protest, then the County Valuation Protests Board.
new-mexico.appeal_how: File the protest form with the county assessor's office within 30 days; if the assessor does not resolve it, the independent three-member County Valuation Protests Board hears the case.
new-mexico.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; New Mexico assesses residential property at one-third of market value.
new-mexico.after_appeal: Appeal the Valuation Protests Board's decision to district court within 30 days of the board's order.

new-york.appeal_deadline: File Form RP-524 with your assessor or Board of Assessment Review by Grievance Day - usually the fourth Tuesday in May in most towns and cities; New York City deadlines are March 1 (Classes 2, 3, and 4) and March 15 (Class 1), and Nassau County has its own window.
new-york.appeal_where: Local assessor for an informal review, then your city or town Board of Assessment Review; New York City uses the Tax Commission and Nassau County uses the Assessment Review Commission.
new-york.appeal_how: File Form RP-524 (Complaint on Real Property Assessment) with the assessor or Board of Assessment Review; it must be received by Grievance Day, not just mailed, and the board issues a written determination.
new-york.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; the form separates unequal, excessive, unlawful, and misclassified assessments.
new-york.appeal_fee: No fee to file Form RP-524; Small Claims Assessment Review (SCAR) costs $30.
new-york.after_appeal: Owner-occupants of one-, two-, or three-family homes may file a Small Claims Assessment Review (SCAR) petition, or any owner may bring an Article 7 tax certiorari case in State Supreme Court, within 30 days of the filing of the final assessment roll.

north-carolina.appeal_deadline: Ask the county Board of Equalization and Review for a hearing before it adjourns; the board first meets between the first Monday in April and the first Monday in May and usually finishes within about three weeks (it may sit until July 1, or December 1 in a revaluation year).
north-carolina.appeal_where: County tax assessor for an informal review, then the county Board of Equalization and Review.
north-carolina.appeal_how: Request an informal review with the assessor within 30 days of your notice, then file a formal appeal with the Board of Equalization and Review before it adjourns; the board must mail its decision within 30 days of adjourning.
north-carolina.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; the value tested is market value on January 1 of the county's last revaluation year.
north-carolina.after_appeal: Appeal to the North Carolina Property Tax Commission within 30 days of the date the board mailed its decision (Form AV-14); a Commission decision can then be appealed to the Court of Appeals within 30 days.

north-dakota.appeal_deadline: Appeal to your local (city or township) Board of Equalization, which meets in April - city boards meet within the first 15 days of April and township boards meet on the second Monday in April; contact your assessor before April 1 to start.
north-dakota.appeal_where: Local assessor first, then the local Board of Equalization, then the County Board of Equalization.
north-dakota.appeal_how: Contact the local assessor before April 1, then appear before the local Board of Equalization in April with your evidence; the County Board of Equalization meets within the first 10 days of June.
north-dakota.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; North Dakota assesses at 50% of market value as of February 1.
north-dakota.after_appeal: If you appeared before both the local and county boards, you may appeal to the State Board of Equalization, which meets the second Tuesday in August; you may also file a formal abatement by November 1 of the year after the tax becomes delinquent, or appeal to district court within 30 days of the county commissioners' decision.

ohio.appeal_deadline: File a complaint with your county Board of Revision between January 1 and March 31 of the year after the tax year (or by the last day to pay first-half taxes, if later); the window is the same in every county.
ohio.appeal_where: County auditor for an informal review, then the county Board of Revision, filed with the county auditor.
ohio.appeal_how: File Form DTE 1 (Complaint Against the Valuation of Real Property) with the county auditor; the board must hear and decide the complaint within 180 days after the filing deadline.
ohio.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal (especially a recent arm's-length sale of your own home), photos of condition or defects, and errors in the auditor's records; Ohio assesses at 35% of true value.
ohio.after_appeal: Within 30 days after the board's decision is mailed, appeal to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or, if you are the owner, to the county Court of Common Pleas instead.

oklahoma.appeal_deadline: File a written informal protest (OTC Form 974) with your county assessor within 30 calendar days of the date your Notice of Change of Value was mailed; if your value did not change and you got no notice, you may protest by the first Monday in April.
oklahoma.appeal_where: County assessor for the informal protest, then the County Board of Equalization.
oklahoma.appeal_how: File Form 974 with the assessor; the assessor must hold an informal hearing and issue a written decision within seven calendar days of the hearing.
oklahoma.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; Oklahoma assesses real property at 11% of fair cash value.
oklahoma.after_appeal: File a formal appeal (OTC Form 976) with the County Board of Equalization within 15 calendar days of the date the assessor's decision was mailed; the board's decision can then be appealed to district court within 30 days.

oregon.appeal_deadline: File a petition with your county Property Value Appeals Board (PVAB) after tax statements are mailed in late October and no later than December 31 (or the next business day if December 31 falls on a weekend or holiday).
oregon.appeal_where: County assessor for an informal review, then the county Property Value Appeals Board (formerly called the Board of Property Tax Appeals), filed with the county clerk.
oregon.appeal_how: File the PVAB petition with your county clerk's office; the board considers appeals between the first Monday in February and April 15.
oregon.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales supporting a lower real market value, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; an appeal only lowers your bill if the corrected real market value falls below your maximum assessed value.
oregon.appeal_fee: Some counties charge a small filing fee; the amount varies by county and was not confirmed statewide.
oregon.after_appeal: Appeal a PVAB decision to the Magistrate Division of the Oregon Tax Court within 30 days of the date the board's order was mailed or delivered; a magistrate decision can then go to the Regular Division of the Tax Court.

pennsylvania.appeal_deadline: Pennsylvania has no single statewide deadline: most counties require annual appeals by August 1, others use September 1 (the statutory default), Allegheny County runs a July 3 to September 1 window, and Philadelphia's Board of Revision of Taxes deadline is the first Monday in October; a new assessment notice gives you 40 days from its mailing.
pennsylvania.appeal_where: County assessment office for an informal review, then the county Board of Assessment Appeals.
pennsylvania.appeal_how: File your county's appeal application with the Board of Assessment Appeals by your county's deadline; the board holds a hearing and decides the market value, then applies the county's common level ratio.
pennsylvania.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessment records; argue market value, since the county's common level ratio is applied separately.
pennsylvania.appeal_fee: Fees vary by county (for example, Dauphin County charges $25 for a single-family home and $100 for apartment and other non-single-family appeals).
pennsylvania.after_appeal: Appeal the board's decision to the Court of Common Pleas within 30 days of the date of the board's decision notice.

rhode-island.appeal_deadline: File an appeal with your city or town tax assessor on or before November 15 of each year, but not less than 90 days after the first tax payment is due.
rhode-island.appeal_where: Local tax assessor first, then the local Tax Board of Review.
rhode-island.appeal_how: File the state-approved appeal application with the local office of tax assessment; the assessor has until December 31 to review it, decide, and notify you.
rhode-island.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal effective on the December 31 assessment date, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records.
rhode-island.after_appeal: If the assessor denies the appeal or does not decide by December 31, appeal to the local Tax Board of Review within 30 days of the assessor's decision (or by January 31 if there was no decision); the board's decision can then go to Superior Court.

south-carolina.appeal_deadline: File a written objection with your county assessor within 90 days after the assessor mails the assessment notice; in a year with no notice, you may appeal at any time, and filing before the first penalty date (January 15) applies it to the current tax year.
south-carolina.appeal_where: County assessor first (written objection and conference), then the County Board of Assessment Appeals.
south-carolina.appeal_how: Give the assessor written notice of objection, then request a conference; if it is not resolved, file a formal written protest within 30 days of the assessor's written response.
south-carolina.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; counties reassess on a five-year cycle and owner-occupied homes are assessed at 4% of fair market value.
south-carolina.appeal_fee: No fee; a written objection to the county assessor is free.
south-carolina.after_appeal: Appeal the assessor's decision to the County Board of Assessment Appeals within 30 days of the assessor's written response; the board's decision can then go to the South Carolina Administrative Law Court within 30 days.

south-dakota.appeal_deadline: Notify the clerk of your local Board of Equalization of your appeal no later than the Thursday before the third Monday in March; assessment notices are mailed by March 1.
south-dakota.appeal_where: Local assessor or director of equalization first, then the local (township or municipal) Board of Equalization, then the County Board of Equalization.
south-dakota.appeal_how: File or mail a written notice of appeal to the clerk of the local board; the local board meets on the third Monday in March.
south-dakota.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; South Dakota assesses residential property at 85% of market value as of January 1.
south-dakota.after_appeal: Appeal the local board's decision to the County Board of Equalization by filing a written notice with the county auditor on or before the first Tuesday in April; the county board meets in April, and its decision can then go to circuit court.

tennessee.appeal_deadline: Appeal to your County Board of Equalization by the deadline printed on your assessment notice - the board convenes June 1 each year (May 1 in Shelby County) and the deadline is typically around June 15 in a reappraisal year; missing it can make the assessment final.
tennessee.appeal_where: County assessor for an informal review, then the County Board of Equalization.
tennessee.appeal_how: Request an informal review with the assessor, then file a formal complaint with the County Board of Equalization before it adjourns; you must appeal to the county board to preserve the right to go further.
tennessee.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; Tennessee taxes homes at 25% of appraised value.
tennessee.after_appeal: Appeal to the State Board of Equalization by August 1 of the tax year or within 45 days of the date the county board's decision notice was sent, whichever is later; the State Board's decision can then go to Chancery or Circuit Court within 60 days of its final order.

texas.appeal_deadline: File a protest with your county appraisal district by May 15, or within 30 days after the district mails your Notice of Appraised Value, whichever is later.
texas.appeal_where: County appraisal district for an informal conference, then the Appraisal Review Board (ARB).
texas.appeal_how: File a written notice of protest (Comptroller Form 50-132) with the appraisal district; you may request an informal conference first, and if that fails the ARB holds a formal hearing.
texas.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or damage, repair estimates, and errors in the district's property records; you can also protest on unequal appraisal - that similar homes are valued lower than yours.
texas.after_appeal: Within 60 days of receiving the ARB's written order, appeal to district court or choose binding arbitration; an appeal to the State Office of Administrative Hearings is available for qualifying property over $1 million within 30 days.

utah.appeal_deadline: Apply to your county Board of Equalization by the later of September 15 or 45 days after the mailing date on your Notice of Property Valuation and Tax Changes (notices arrive in July or August).
utah.appeal_where: County assessor for an informal review, then the county Board of Equalization (the county legislative body sitting as the board), filed with the county auditor or clerk.
utah.appeal_how: File your appeal application with the county Board of Equalization; the board must decide within 60 days of your application.
utah.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; the value is fair market value as of January 1.
utah.after_appeal: Appeal to the Utah State Tax Commission within 30 days of the Board of Equalization's decision, by filing with the county auditor; the Commission's decision can then go to District Court or the Utah Supreme Court.

vermont.appeal_deadline: Grievance deadlines are set by each town: when your appraisal changes, the listers mail a change notice and you have 14 days from the mailing date to grieve; grievance hearings are generally held in late spring (April to June).
vermont.appeal_where: Town listers (or assessor) for a grievance, then the town Board of Civil Authority (BCA), filed with the town clerk.
vermont.appeal_how: File a written grievance with the listers on or before the grievance meeting date and appear at the hearing; if the listers do not adjust the value, appeal in writing to the BCA through the town clerk.
vermont.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales as of the April 1 assessment date, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the listers' records; the BCA appoints a three-member committee to inspect your property.
vermont.after_appeal: Appeal the BCA's decision within 30 days to the state Director of Property Valuation and Review (a state appraiser) or to the county Superior Court - you choose one.

virginia.appeal_deadline: Virginia has no statewide deadline: each city or county sets its own Board of Equalization deadline, usually between April 30 and July 1 (for example, Fairfax and Loudoun June 1, Prince William July 1 in 2026); the date is printed on your assessment notice.
virginia.appeal_where: Local assessor or Commissioner of the Revenue for an administrative review, then the local Board of Equalization.
virginia.appeal_how: Request an administrative review with the assessor first, then file an application with the Board of Equalization by your locality's deadline; the board is a citizen panel appointed by the Circuit Court.
virginia.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records.
virginia.after_appeal: Appeal the Board of Equalization's decision to Circuit Court within 30 days; you may also skip the board and apply directly to Circuit Court, generally within three years of the end of the tax year.

washington.appeal_deadline: File a petition with your county Board of Equalization by July 1 of the assessment year, or within 30 days after your value change notice was mailed, whichever is later; some counties allow up to 60 days by local ordinance.
washington.appeal_where: County assessor for an informal review, then the county Board of Equalization.
washington.appeal_how: File a taxpayer petition (Department of Revenue Form 64 0075) with the Board of Equalization in the county where the property sits; the board holds a hearing and issues a written decision.
washington.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; the assessor's value is presumed correct, so the burden is on you.
washington.appeal_fee: No fee to file a petition with the county Board of Equalization.
washington.after_appeal: Appeal the county board's decision to the Washington State Board of Tax Appeals within 30 days of the mailing date of the county board's decision.

west-virginia.appeal_deadline: File a written protest with the county commission sitting as a Board of Equalization and Review no later than February 20 of the tax year; the board begins meeting February 1 and must adjourn by February 28.
west-virginia.appeal_where: County assessor for an informal review (notify the assessor within 8 business days of receiving your notice), then the County Commission sitting as a Board of Equalization and Review.
west-virginia.appeal_how: Contact the assessor for an informal review within 8 business days of your notice, then file a written protest with the clerk of the county commission by February 20, stating the value in dispute and your reasons.
west-virginia.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records.
west-virginia.after_appeal: Appeal the board's decision to the West Virginia Office of Tax Appeals or to Circuit Court within 30 days of the decision.

wisconsin.appeal_deadline: Wisconsin has no single statewide date: first talk to your assessor at Open Book, then object to your municipal Board of Review - you must tell the board's clerk at least 48 hours before the board's first meeting and file your written objection before that meeting or within its first two hours; dates are set by each municipality, mostly in spring through fall.
wisconsin.appeal_where: Municipal assessor at Open Book, then the municipal Board of Review.
wisconsin.appeal_how: Meet the assessor at Open Book to discuss the value, then give the board clerk at least 48 hours' notice and file a written objection on the state form; the board holds a hearing and decides.
wisconsin.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales, an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records.
wisconsin.after_appeal: If the board denies your objection, you may appeal further - the board's written decision states the deadline and the route (the Department of Revenue or circuit court).

wyoming.appeal_deadline: File a written statement with your county assessor no later than 30 days after the date the assessment schedule was mailed (schedules go out by the fourth Monday in April).
wyoming.appeal_where: County assessor first, then the County Board of Equalization (the county commissioners sitting as that board).
wyoming.appeal_how: File a written statement with the assessor giving your reasons; the assessor forwards a copy to the county clerk, and both sides exchange evidence at least 30 days before the county board hearing.
wyoming.appeal_evidence: Comparable sales (from statements of consideration), an appraisal, photos of condition or defects, and errors in the assessor's records; the appeal must address market value, not the tax rate.
wyoming.after_appeal: Appeal the County Board of Equalization's decision to the Wyoming State Board of Equalization within 30 days of the decision (or of its mailing, whichever is later); the State Board's decision can then go to district court.
